title: Coordination and the Neuron
summary: Why animals need coordination, the nervous and endocrine systems compared, and the structure and kinds of neuron.

p: Living things must detect changes (stimuli) inside and outside the body and respond correctly so that the body stays balanced (homeostasis). In animals, two systems work together to do this.

The nervous system sends fast electrical messages that act quickly and last a short time. The endocrine system sends chemical messages (hormones) in the blood that act slowly and last longer. Compare them: nervous messages travel along nerves, are very fast (milliseconds), act on a small area (a muscle or gland) and stop quickly, for example pulling your hand from a hot pot. Hormonal messages travel in the blood, are slow (seconds to hours), may act on many organs and may last a long time, for example growth hormone or insulin.
The nervous system contains billions of nerve cells called neurons, supported by glial cells (neuroglia), which feed and protect them.

img.alt: A labelled diagram of a motor neuron with the dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier and synaptic knobs

p: Cell body (soma): has the nucleus, many mitochondria for energy and Nissl granules (groups of ribosomes that make proteins). Dendrites: short, much-branched fibres that receive messages and carry them towards the cell body. Axon: one long fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body; its cytoplasm is the axoplasm and its membrane is the axolemma. Myelin sheath: a fatty insulating layer made by Schwann cells (in nerves) or oligodendrocytes (in the brain and spinal cord); it stops the signal leaking out and makes it faster. Nodes of Ranvier: gaps in the myelin where the axon membrane is exposed. Synaptic knobs: swellings at the end of the axon that contain vesicles full of chemicals called neurotransmitters.

Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors (skin, eyes, ears) to the central nervous system (CNS); the cell body sits to one side (unipolar). Motor (efferent) neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands); they are multipolar. Relay neurons (interneurons) lie wholly in the CNS and link sensory to motor neurons and process information. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is all the nerves outside.

title: How a Nerve Impulse Travels and Crosses a Synapse
summary: The resting potential, the action potential, saltatory conduction and synaptic transmission with neurotransmitters.

sections.h: A nerve impulse is not an electric current in a wire
p: It is a travelling wave of electrical and chemical change along the surface of the axon, much slower than a current in a wire.

A neuron at rest is like a charged battery: the inside of the axon is negative (about –70 mV) compared with the outside. This is called polarised. It happens because (1) the membrane lets potassium ions (K⁺) leak out much more easily than sodium ions (Na⁺) leak in, and (2) the sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to push 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ it brings in. More positive charge is therefore outside than inside.
When a stimulus is strong enough to reach the threshold (about –55 mV), the following happens in order:
1. Depolarisation: voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ rushes in. The inside quickly becomes positive (about +40 mV).
2. Repolarisation: sodium channels close and potassium channels open, so K⁺ rushes out and the inside becomes negative again.

3. Hyperpolarisation: potassium channels stay open slightly too long, so the inside becomes a little more negative than the resting level (about –80 mV) for a moment. The pump then restores the resting state.
4. Refractory period: for a short time the neuron cannot fire again. This makes the impulse move in one direction only.
All-or-none law: a stimulus below the threshold produces no impulse; at or above the threshold, a full-size impulse always occurs. A stronger stimulus gives more frequent impulses, not bigger ones.

img.alt: A graph of an action potential showing resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation and hyperpolarisation, and the movement of sodium and potassium ions

p: In a myelinated axon the ions cannot cross the fatty sheath, so the action potential occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse seems to 'jump' from node to node. This saltatory conduction raises the speed from about 2 m/s in unmyelinated fibres to as much as 120 m/s, and it saves energy.
A synapse is the junction between two neurons (the gap is about 20 nm wide, a thousand times thinner than a hair). The impulse cannot jump the gap electrically, so a chemical does it.

img.alt: A synapse showing the pre-synaptic knob with vesicles, the synaptic cleft and receptors on the post-synaptic membrane

p: 1. The impulse reaches the pre-synaptic knob. 2. Calcium ions (Ca²⁺) enter through voltage-gated channels. 3. The calcium makes vesicles join the membrane and release the neurotransmitter into the cleft (exocytosis). 4. The neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane. 5. Ion channels open and a new action potential starts in the next neuron. 6. An enzyme (for example acetylcholinesterase) breaks down the neurotransmitter so that it does not fire again and again.

Common neurotransmitters: acetylcholine (muscle contraction and many nerves), dopamine (reward and movement), serotonin (mood and sleep). A synapse allows messages to travel in one direction only, and lets one neuron combine signals from many others. Some drugs and poisons act here: curare blocks acetylcholine receptors, and organophosphate pesticides block acetylcholinesterase, so they are dangerous to farmers.

title: The Central Nervous System: Brain and Spinal Cord
summary: The protection of the CNS, the parts of the brain and their jobs, and the structure of the spinal cord.

p: The brain is protected by the skull and the spinal cord by the vertebral column (backbone). Both are wrapped in three membranes called the meninges (outer dura mater, middle arachnoid, inner pia mater) with a cushioning cerebrospinal fluid. Infection of the meninges is called meningitis, a danger well known in northern Nigeria.

Forebrain: The cerebrum has a left and right hemisphere. Its outer layer, the cerebral cortex, is grey matter (cell bodies) and the inner part is white matter (axons). It is folded to give a large surface area for more neurons. It controls thinking, memory, learning, speech, vision, hearing and voluntary movement. The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex. The hypothalamus is the control centre for homeostasis: temperature, water balance, hunger, and it controls the pituitary gland.
Midbrain: includes the optic lobes that control visual reflexes such as the size of the pupil.

Hindbrain: the cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, posture and balance; if it is damaged the person has jerky, unsteady movements and loses balance (ataxia). The medulla oblongata controls vital involuntary actions: heart beat, breathing rate, swallowing, coughing, vomiting and peristalsis.

img.alt: A side view of the human brain with the cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, cerebellum and medulla oblongata labelled

p: A cylinder of nervous tissue running inside the backbone. In cross-section its arrangement is the opposite of the brain's: the grey matter is inside in an H or butterfly shape, and the white matter (axons) is on the outside. A small hole in the centre, the central canal, contains fluid.

Each spinal nerve joins the cord by two roots: the dorsal (back) root carries sensory impulses into the cord and has a swelling, the dorsal root ganglion, with the sensory cell bodies; the ventral (front) root carries motor impulses out to the muscles. The spinal cord carries messages up to the brain and down from it, and controls reflex actions.

title: The Peripheral and Autonomic Nervous System and Reflex Actions
summary: Cranial and spinal nerves, the somatic and autonomic systems, sympathetic and parasympathetic control, and the reflex arc.

p: The PNS joins the CNS to the rest of the body. It has 12 pairs of cranial nerves (from the brain, for example the optic nerve and the vagus nerve) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (from the spinal cord).

The somatic system controls voluntary actions of the skeletal muscles (writing, walking). The autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls involuntary actions of internal organs (heart, gut, glands, bladder) without conscious thought.
The ANS has two opposite parts. The sympathetic system prepares the body for 'fight or flight' (a man sees a snake and runs). The parasympathetic system is for 'rest and digest'.

When a man sees a snake, the sympathetic system works together with adrenaline from the adrenal glands: the heart beats faster, the breathing is quicker and deeper, the pupils widen, the blood vessels to the gut narrow and those to the muscles widen, the liver releases glucose, and the body sweats. All these supply muscles with energy and oxygen to run or fight.

A reflex is a fast, automatic response to a stimulus, which does not need thinking. The path is the reflex arc: receptor (detects the stimulus, for example heat) → sensory neuron (through the dorsal root) → relay neuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord → motor neuron (leaves through the ventral root) → effector (a muscle that contracts, pulling the hand away). Because the arc goes through the spinal cord only, the response is very fast and the brain is bypassed; the brain is told afterwards, so we feel the pain a little later.

img.alt: A reflex arc in the spinal cord from a hand touching a hot object to a muscle contracting

p: Simple (unconditioned) reflexes are inborn: knee-jerk, blinking, pupil reflex, sneezing, withdrawing the hand. A conditioned reflex is learned by association: in Pavlov's experiment dogs learned to salivate at the sound of a bell that was rung with food. A conditioned reflex needs the cerebrum because the brain must learn the link; a simple reflex does not. (Skills such as cycling are learned habits, not true reflexes, but they also use the cerebrum and cerebellum.)
Reflex: fast, automatic, no thinking, passes through the spinal cord. Voluntary: slower, needs thought, involves the cerebrum.

title: The Eye: Structure and How We See
summary: Sense organs as transducers, the layers and parts of the eye, rods and cones, the blind spot and how an image is formed.

p: Sense organs are our windows to the world. They contain receptors that change (transduce) light, sound, pressure and chemicals into nerve impulses for the brain. A stimulus is a detectable change; a receptor detects it; an effector (a muscle or gland) responds.
The eye is a fluid-filled ball protected by the bony socket (orbit), eyelids and tears.

Outer layer: the sclera is the tough white of the eye, which keeps the shape and protects. The cornea is the clear front window, with no blood vessels so it stays clear; it gets oxygen from the air and does about two thirds of the bending of light. The conjunctiva is a thin transparent membrane over the sclera and inside the eyelids; infection causes conjunctivitis (in Nigeria, the red-eye type is popularly called 'Apollo').

Middle layer: the choroid has many blood vessels and dark pigment; it feeds the retina and absorbs stray light so that vision is not blurred. The ciliary body has ciliary muscles that change the shape of the lens, and ciliary processes that make the aqueous humour. Suspensory ligaments hold the lens. The iris is the coloured muscular ring whose hole, the pupil, controls how much light enters.

Inner layer: the retina contains the light-sensitive cells. Rods (about 120 million) work in dim light, contain rhodopsin (visual purple) and give black and white vision and detect movement; they are at the edges. Cones (about 6 million) work in bright light, give colour vision and sharp detail, and are mostly at the centre. The fovea (yellow spot) has only cones and is the point of sharpest vision. The blind spot (optic disc) is where the optic nerve leaves; it has no receptors.

img.alt: A labelled section of the human eye showing the cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, suspensory ligaments, retina, fovea, blind spot, optic nerve and humours
img.cap: The structure of the human eye.

p: Aqueous humour: a watery fluid between the cornea and lens that keeps the eye pressure steady and feeds the cornea and lens. Lens: a clear, elastic, biconvex structure that changes shape to focus light. Vitreous humour: a clear jelly filling the large chamber behind the lens, which holds the retina against the choroid and keeps the eyeball round.

Light passes through the cornea, aqueous humour, pupil, lens and vitreous humour to the retina. These parts bend (refract) the rays to focus them on the retina. The image on the retina is real, upside-down and smaller than the object. The rods and cones make impulses that travel along the optic nerve to the brain (the visual area of the cerebrum), which turns the picture the right way up.

When you walk from bright sunlight into a dark cinema hall, you cannot see for a minute or two, because the rods in the retina have been bleached by strong light. In the dark, rhodopsin is rebuilt slowly, and the rods become sensitive again, so you gradually see. The pupil also widens at once.

title: Accommodation, the Pupil Reflex and Defects of the Eye
summary: How the lens focuses on near and far objects, how the pupil changes size, and the causes and correction of short sight, long sight, astigmatism and presbyopia.

p: Accommodation is the automatic adjustment of the lens to see things at different distances. The ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments work in opposite ways.

Bright light: the circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil gets smaller. This stops dazzling and protects the retina. Dim light: the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax, so the pupil widens to let in more light. This is a reflex controlled by the midbrain.

Myopia (short-sightedness): near objects are clear but distant ones are blurred. The eyeball is too long, or the lens is too strong. The image forms in front of the retina. It is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.

Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): distant objects are clear but near ones are blurred. The eyeball is too short, or the lens is too weak. The image forms behind the retina. It is corrected with a convex (converging) lens.
Astigmatism: the cornea or lens is not evenly curved, so the image is distorted; corrected with cylindrical lenses.
Presbyopia: in old age the lens loses its elasticity and cannot focus on near things; corrected with reading glasses or bifocal lenses.

img.alt: Diagrams of a normal eye, a short-sighted eye corrected with a concave lens, and a long-sighted eye corrected with a convex lens
img.cap: Short sight and long sight, and their correction.

p: Cataract: the lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision; it is treated by replacing the lens in surgery. Glaucoma: the pressure in the eye rises and damages the optic nerve, causing loss of side vision; it is treated with drops or surgery. Night blindness: caused by lack of vitamin A, so eat carrots, palm oil (red oil), liver and green leaves. Cheap checks and early treatment can prevent blindness.

Predators such as lions and owls have both eyes at the front, giving binocular vision and a good judgement of distance. Prey animals such as antelopes and rabbits have eyes at the sides for a very wide field of view to spot danger.

title: The Ear: Hearing and Balance
summary: The parts of the outer, middle and inner ear, how sound becomes nerve impulses, and how the ear keeps balance.

p: The ear has two jobs: hearing and balance.

img.alt: A cross-section of the human ear showing the pinna, ear canal, eardrum, ossicles, Eustachian tube, cochlea, semicircular canals and auditory nerve

p: Pinna (auricle): a flap of cartilage that collects sound. Auditory canal: a tube with hairs and wax glands that trap dust and insects. Eardrum (tympanic membrane): a thin membrane that vibrates when sound arrives and separates the outer from the middle ear.

An air-filled space in the skull bone. The three smallest bones in the body, the ossicles, are the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil) and stapes (stirrup), in that order from the eardrum. They pass the vibrations to the oval window and make them about 20 times stronger. The Eustachian tube joins the middle ear to the throat and opens when you swallow or yawn, so that the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum is equal. If it is blocked (for example by a cold), the ears hurt in an aeroplane.

A fluid-filled maze (labyrinth) in the bone. The cochlea is a coiled tube with the Organ of Corti (the receptor for hearing). The vestibular apparatus is for balance: three semicircular canals at right angles to each other, and the utricle and saccule, chambers that hold otoliths.

1. The pinna collects sound waves into the canal. 2. The waves hit the eardrum and make it vibrate. 3. The ossicles vibrate and amplify the force; the stapes pushes like a piston on the oval window. 4. This makes pressure waves in the fluid of the cochlea. 5. The waves move the basilar membrane, and the hair cells of the Organ of Corti are bent against the tectorial membrane. 6. The bending makes nerve impulses that go along the auditory nerve to the brain. 7. The pressure is released through the round window.

Dynamic balance (movement of the head): when the head turns, the fluid in the semicircular canals lags behind and bends the hair cells of the cupula, telling the brain the direction and speed of rotation. Static balance (position): in the utricle and saccule, tiny crystals of calcium carbonate (otoliths) are pulled by gravity when the head tilts and bend the hair cells. Dizziness after spinning happens because the fluid keeps moving after you stop.

title: Nose, Tongue and Skin: Smell, Taste and Touch
summary: Chemoreceptors for smell and taste, the real facts about the tongue, the receptors in the skin and why a cold spoils taste.

p: The olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity contains chemoreceptors that detect gas molecules dissolved in the mucus. Smell is much more sensitive than taste, and it is closely linked with the part of the brain that stores memory and emotion, which is why a smell can bring back a memory.
Taste buds are in small bumps called papillae. They detect chemicals dissolved in saliva. The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami (savoury, as in meat, crayfish and seasoning).

A correction: the old 'tongue map' (sweet at the tip, sour at the sides, bitter at the back) is a myth. Every taste can be sensed on all parts of the tongue that have taste buds, although some places are a little more sensitive. What we call flavour is taste plus smell plus texture and temperature.

sections.h: Why food tastes bland with a cold
p: With a blocked nose, the smell molecules cannot reach the olfactory cells, so the flavour is lost even though taste buds still work. Pinch your nose while eating a sweet and notice how the flavour changes.

The skin is the largest organ and has many types of receptors: mechanoreceptors, such as Meissner's corpuscles for light touch and Pacinian corpuscles for deep pressure and vibration; thermoreceptors, for warmth and cold; and nociceptors (free nerve endings) for pain. Pain is useful because it warns us of damage. Some body parts, such as the fingertips and lips, have many more receptors, so they are more sensitive than the back.
Compare the senses.
